pr_title: remote: verify hash of download blobs. fixes #7169
pr_comments:
I’m sorry if this question is really dumb but why do we need a cryptographic hash here? Is it because we don’t want someone to maliciously poison the cache?
Reason I’m asking is that for our use case what we’re mainly concerned about is network issues.

@ittaiz it's not about malicious intent but simply about verifying that what we got is what we requested. Pretty much any http server can serve as a remote cache for Bazel and there's plenty of opportunity for files to get corrupted and this is a simple defensive measure.
I definitely agree. My question was why we need a *cryptographic* hash?

@ittaiz Because the cache is a content-addressable storage system, which means we're deduplicating data purely based on their hash. If you don't want to protect against insiders poisoning your cache with malicious artifacts, you'd still want to minimize the chance of accidental collisions, because that would break your build and cache.

As an example, ZFS, which also supports deduplication, only allows you to do it based on the checksum when you use cryptographic hashes, e.g. SHA256, SHA512, Skein or Edon-R. Other hashes are not seen as safe enough and require a byte-for-byte comparison in case of a collision, which ZFS can do, but a CAS cannot.

👍🏽 thanks for the explanation
@benjaminp aren’t you concerned about network issues corrupting the outputs?

> @benjaminp aren’t you concerned about network issues corrupting the outputs?

TCP/IP has checksums, so not particularly, no. #7169, which prompted this change, involved manually corrupting the cache.

I see, thanks!

issue_context.title: Neither Bazel or Bazel-Remote verifies the sha256 when GET files from server
issue_context.body:
Step to reproduce:
Use https://github.com/bazelbuild/examples and build with Bazel-Remote cache. In the cache server modify one of the files in CAS folder and verify the sha256 indeed changed using "openssl dgst -sha256", then build again. You can notice when Bazel-Remote get the modified file, you can see it just returns 200 and the build succeeds.

Question is how it can ensure the correctness of the final build output?
comments: @bayareabear which version of Bazel are you using? We do have code that is expected to verify that the digests match, but it's possible that it's broken.

I am using the following version:
xzhang3$ bazel version
INFO: Invocation ID: 7e7aca66-bb36-4374-af0b-5954e1e267ad
Build label: 0.21.0
Is the check on every AC and CAS entry or just some of them? I just randomly modified one CAS entry?
